etymology: From Latin punire, to inflict penalty, from poena, penalty, pain. Webster 1828: to pain, to afflict with pain, loss, or calamity for a crime or fault. Scripture reserves the word almost entirely for God’s own act as Judge, and for the magistrate acting under Him.
biblical_def: Punish in Scripture is chiefly what God does, and the striking thing about the biblical use is where He begins. Amos states the principle that governs the whole prophetic literature: You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities (Amos 3:2). The therefore is the shock. Nearness to God is not an exemption from judgment but the ground of it, and the same logic runs through judgment must begin at the house of God (1 Peter 4:17). Isaiah widens it to the whole world and names the target precisely: I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible (Isaiah 13:11). Zephaniah reaches men whose offence is not violence but settled indifference: I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil (Zephaniah 1:12). Wine left on its dregs grows thick and flat, and the figure describes a man too comfortable to expect anything from God at all — and God searches for him with lamps.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PUNISH as to pain; to afflict with pain, loss, or calamity for a crime or fault; primarily to afflict with bodily pain, but extended to any penalty inflicted by authority for the violation of law.
webster_full: PUNISH, v.t. — To pain; to afflict with pain, loss, or calamity for a crime or fault.
To inflict a penalty on, by authority, for the violation of a law, whether human or divine.
Punishment is inflicted by the offended party or by lawful authority; revenge is taken by a private person, and is forbidden.
To chastise; as, a father punishes his child for disobedience — though here the end is correction rather than retribution.
From Latin poena, penalty — the root also of penal, penalty, penance, and pain.
scriptures: Amos 3:2
You only have I known of all the families of the earth: therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.
Isaiah 13:11
And I will punish the world for their evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; and I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease, and will lay low the haughtiness of the terrible.
Zephaniah 1:12

And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.
Proverbs 11:21
Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered.
corruption_summary: Modern religious sentiment has largely retired the idea that God punishes at all, reassigning every judgment to natural consequence, and the therapeutic reframing of sin as harm rather than guilt removes the only category in which punishment makes sense.
corruption_paragraphs: The consequence-only account — that God does not punish but simply allows sin to work its own ruin — has the appearance of mercy and the substance of a denial. It cannot survive Isaiah 13:11, where God says I will punish and then names what He will do to the arrogancy of the proud, nor Amos 3:2, where the punishing follows from the knowing. It also empties the cross. If God does not punish sin, then the death of Christ was not a bearing of penalty, and penal substitution collapses into a demonstration of solidarity. The doctrines stand or fall together: a God who does not punish needs no propitiation, and a Saviour who bore no penalty saves from nothing.

The second and subtler corruption redefines sin as harm. Where the primary moral category is damage done to another person or to oneself, an act with no measurable victim ceases to be sin, and God’s interest in it becomes unintelligible. Scripture’s category is guilt before God: David, who had committed adultery and arranged a murder, says Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight (Psalm 51:4). He does not mean Uriah was unharmed; he means the offence that requires atonement is offence against God. Zephaniah 1:12 shows how far this reaches — men who had harmed no one, settled on their lees, saying in their hearts that the LORD would do neither good nor evil, and God searching the city with candles to find them.
roots_summary: Hebrew paqad (H6485), to visit, to muster, to punish; naqam (H5358), to avenge; Greek kolazo (G2849), to punish, to chastise; ekdikeo (G1556), to vindicate, to punish judicially.
roots_lines: Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to attend to, to punish; the same verb covers God’s visiting in mercy and in judgment (Amos 3:2; Exodus 20:5).
Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; reserved to God and to the magistrate He appoints.
Greek kolazo (G2849) — to punish, to correct; the Lord knoweth how… to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished (2 Peter 2:9).
Greek kolasis (G2851) — punishment; these shall go away into everlasting punishment (Matthew 25:46).
Greek ekdikeo (G1556) — to execute justice on behalf of; the root of the magistrate’s office in Romans 13:4.
usage: You only have I known… therefore I will punish you (Amos 3:2) — nearness to God as the ground of judgment, not exemption from it.
I will cause the arrogancy of the proud to cease (Isaiah 13:11) — the named target of the world’s punishment.
Punish the men that are settled on their lees (Zephaniah 1:12) — God searching a city with candles for the comfortably indifferent.

etymology: From un- (not) and punished. Webster 1828: not punished; suffered to pass without punishment. In the Authorized Version it appears almost exclusively in a negative construction — shall not be unpunished — a double negative that functions as a strong affirmation.
biblical_def: Unpunished occurs in Scripture chiefly to be denied. Proverbs uses the double negative for emphasis, and the emphasis is the point: Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered (Proverbs 11:21). Hand join in hand pictures conspiracy, mutual pledge, the confederacy of the wicked reinforcing one another — and the numbers change nothing. Twice more the same construction lands on the man who lies in a court: A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape (Proverbs 19:5). Perjury is singled out because a false witness turns the very instrument of justice into the instrument of murder, as it did at Naboth’s trial and at Christ’s. The word takes a different and more tender turn in Jeremiah, where God speaks to His own people in exile: I am with thee, saith the LORD, to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee: but I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished (Jeremiah 30:11). Not left unpunished, and not made a full end of — correction in measure is what distinguishes a son from a stranger.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UNPUNISHED as not punished; suffered to escape the penalty due to an offence; free from punishment.
webster_full: UNPUNISHED, a. — Not punished; suffered to pass without the infliction of a penalty.
Free from punishment, whether by pardon, by neglect of authority, or by escape.
In Scripture, most often used in the negative form — shall not be unpunished — which is a strong affirmation that punishment will certainly follow.
Applied both to persons and to the offences themselves; as, the crime went unpunished.
From un-, not, and punished, from Latin poena, penalty.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:21
Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished: but the seed of the righteous shall be delivered.
Proverbs 19:5
A false witness shall not be unpunished, and he that speaketh lies shall not escape.
Jeremiah 30:11

For I am with thee, saith the LORD, to save thee: though I make a full end of all nations whither I have scattered thee, yet will I not make a full end of thee: but I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished.
Proverbs 12:7
The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand.
corruption_summary: The observable fact that much wickedness goes unpunished in this life is the oldest argument against God’s justice, and Scripture answers it not by denying the observation but by insisting the account is not yet closed.
corruption_paragraphs: Asaph states the problem more sharply than any modern sceptic: I was envious at the foolish, when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death… they are not in trouble as other men (Psalm 73:3-5). He does not dispute the data. What changed his judgment was a location: until I went into the sanctuary of God; then understood I their end. The biblical answer to unpunished wickedness is eschatological, and it requires a real final judgment with real and eternal consequence. Remove that — whether by annihilationism, universalism, or a quiet embarrassment about hell — and Proverbs 11:21 becomes untrue, since hand join in hand plainly does succeed in this world, often for a lifetime.

The pastoral counterpart is Jeremiah 30:11, and it needs saying to the other kind of sufferer. God tells a scattered, defeated people that He will not leave them altogether unpunished, and He says it as a mercy in the middle of a promise of salvation. Correction in measure is the mark of sonship; Hebrews 12:8 says that if a man is without chastisement he is not a son. The believer who finds God dealing hardly with him is not being treated as the nations are treated — of them God says He will make a full end. Measured correction and full end are two different things, and the difference is the covenant.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqah (H5352), to be clean, to be held innocent, to go unpunished; paqad (H6485), to visit, to punish; Greek atimoretos, unavenged; ekpheugo (G1628), to escape.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be clean, to be acquitted, to go free; the negative lo yinnaqeh is the shall not be unpunished of Proverbs.
Hebrew naqi (H5355) — innocent, clear; the adjective from the same root, as in innocent blood.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to punish; I will not leave thee altogether unpunished (Jeremiah 30:11).
Greek ekpheugo (G1628) — to flee out, to escape; how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation? (Hebrews 2:3).
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, the verdict rightly given; the standard against which impunity is measured.
usage: Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished (Proverbs 11:21) — conspiracy does not alter the outcome.
A false witness shall not be unpunished (Proverbs 19:5) — perjury singled out, because it turns justice into murder.
I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished (Jeremiah 30:11) — measured correction as the mark of sonship.

etymology: From over and throw, Saxon thrawan, to cast or hurl. Webster 1828: turned over; thrown down; ruined; defeated. In Scripture the word is used of cities, of armies, of houses in the moral sense, and of a whole generation in the wilderness.
biblical_def: Overthrown is what happens to what will not stand, and Scripture applies it at every scale from a household to a generation. Proverbs sets it against endurance twice: The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand (Proverbs 12:7), and The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish (Proverbs 14:11). The contrast is deliberate and humbling: the wicked have a house, solid and built, while the upright have a tabernacle, a tent — and it is the tent that flourishes. Jonah’s five-word sermon uses the word as the whole message: Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown (Jonah 3:4), and the city repented, and God repented of the evil He had said He would do. Paul applies it to Israel in the desert as the standing warning to the church: But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:5). They had all passed through the sea, all eaten the same spiritual meat, all drunk of the Rock — and were overthrown anyway, which is why Paul adds that these things were written for our admonition.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines OVERTHROWN as turned over; thrown down or over; ruined; subverted; defeated; destroyed — applied to buildings, to armies, to governments, and to persons.
webster_full: OVERTHROWN, pp. — Turned over; thrown down; prostrated; demolished.
Defeated; vanquished; routed, as an army in battle.
Ruined; subverted; destroyed, as a city, a state, or a design.
Applied figuratively to persons and to houses in the sense of a family or line brought to nothing.
From over and throw, Saxon thrawan, to cast — the root also of throw and overthrow.
scriptures: Proverbs 12:7
The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand.
Proverbs 14:11
The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish.
Jonah 3:4
And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.
1 Corinthians 10:5
But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness.
corruption_summary: 1 Corinthians 10:5 says that men who had every covenant privilege were overthrown in the wilderness, which is the passage most directly opposed to the popular assurance that a past profession secures a man regardless of how he continues.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s list of what the wilderness generation possessed is deliberately sacramental: all under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all baptized unto Moses, all ate the same spiritual meat, all drank the same spiritual drink, and that Rock was Christ. Then: But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness. The conclusion he draws is let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. This is not a denial of the perseverance of the saints; the Reformed doctrine has always held that those truly regenerate will persevere and that the means of their persevering include exactly such warnings. What it denies is the popular deformation — that a decision recorded years ago settles the question and that continuance is optional. Hebrews 3 and 4 press the same generation for the same reason.

Jonah 3:4 corrects a different error, this time about prophecy. Jonah preached that Nineveh should be overthrown in forty days; Nineveh repented; God did not destroy it; and Jonah was furious precisely because he had expected this. His complaint in chapter 4 is that he knew God to be gracious… and repentest thee of the evil. A prophecy of judgment carries an implicit condition, as Jeremiah 18:7-8 states outright, and this is not a failed prediction but the ordinary way God’s threatenings work. It is worth noting to those who dismiss the prophets as unreliable, and equally to those who preach judgment without ever expecting anyone to repent of it.
roots_summary: Hebrew haphak (H2015), to turn, to overturn — the verb used of Sodom; haras (H2040), to pull down, to break down; Greek katastronnumi (G2693), to strew down, to lay low; kataluo (G2647), to throw down.
roots_lines: Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn over, to overthrow; used of Sodom and Gomorrah and of Nineveh in Jonah 3:4.
Hebrew haras (H2040) — to break down, to demolish; the house of the wicked shall be overthrown (Proverbs 14:11).
Greek katastronnumi (G2693) — to strew down, to lay bodies low over a plain; the vivid verb of 1 Corinthians 10:5.
Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to demolish; Gamaliel’s ye cannot overthrow it (Acts 5:39).
Greek anatrepo (G396) — to overturn; used of those who overthrow the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:18).
usage: The wicked are overthrown, and are not (Proverbs 12:7) — the built house against the standing tent.
Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown (Jonah 3:4) — a threatening that carried its own condition.
They were overthrown in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:5) — every privilege, and no perseverance.

etymology: From destroy, Latin destruere, to unbuild, from de (down) and struere (to build). Webster 1828: one who destroys or lays waste. In Exodus the word names the agent of the tenth plague, and in 1 Corinthians the agent that struck the murmurers.
biblical_def: The destroyer in Scripture is an agent under God’s command, not a rival power, and the Passover text is careful about this. For the LORD will pass through to smite the Egyptians; and when he seeth the blood upon the lintel, and on the two side posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you (Exodus 12:23). Two things are said in one verse: the LORD Himself passes through to smite, and the LORD does not suffer the destroyer to enter where the blood is. The destroyer acts only by permission, and the permission is withheld at every marked door. Paul names the same figure in his catalogue of wilderness judgments: Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10) — murmuring, the sin that seems smallest in the list, is the one with the destroyer attached. Proverbs uses the word for a human character, and the association is bracing: Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer (Proverbs 28:24). The man who steals from his parents and calls it nothing keeps company he has not chosen.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DESTROYER as one who destroys, ruins, kills, or lays waste; a person or agent that demolishes, subverts, or brings to nothing.
webster_full: DESTROYER, n. — One who destroys, ruins, or lays waste; one who kills or puts an end to.
An agent employed in destruction, whether human, angelic, or providential.
One who subverts or brings to nothing; as, the destroyer of a family, a fortune, or a reputation.
In Scripture, the angel employed in the tenth plague and in the judgment of the murmurers.
From Latin destruo, to unbuild, from de and struo, to build — the root also of structure and construct.
scriptures: Exodus 12:23

For the LORD will pass through to smite the Egyptians; and when he seeth the blood upon the lintel, and on the two side posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you.
1 Corinthians 10:10
Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer.
Proverbs 28:24
Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer.
Proverbs 12:7
The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand.
corruption_summary: Dualism — ancient Manichaean, medieval Cathar, and its modern popular form in which Satan is treated as God’s near-equal opponent — makes the destroyer an independent power, when Exodus 12:23 shows him permitted or forbidden entry at God’s word.
corruption_paragraphs: The grammar of Exodus 12:23 will not support two comparable powers. The LORD passes through to smite; the LORD sees the blood; the LORD passes over; and the LORD will not suffer the destroyer to come in. Every verb belongs to God, including the one that governs the destroyer. The same structure appears in Job, where Satan must ask permission twice and is given a boundary each time, and in Luke 22:31, where Satan desires to have the disciples and Christ has already prayed. A popular Christianity that pictures the Christian life as a contest between two roughly matched combatants, with the outcome hanging on the believer’s spiritual technique, has misread the whole doctrine of providence. The devil is a creature on a leash held by the God he hates.

1 Corinthians 10:10 supplies the sting the passage was written to deliver. Of all the wilderness sins Paul lists — idolatry, fornication, tempting Christ — the one he attaches the destroyer to is murmuring. Grumbling feels like the most private and least consequential of sins, a matter of tone rather than substance, and Scripture treats it as a verdict rendered against God’s government. Numbers 14 has the whole generation refused entry for it. The dictionary names this not as a curiosity but as the ordinary besetting sin of comfortable believers, and Philippians 2:14 gives the plain command: Do all things without murmurings and disputings.
roots_summary: Hebrew mashchith (H4889), a destroyer, a ruin; shachath (H7843), to spoil, to ruin; Greek olothreutes (G3644), the destroyer; Apollyon (G623), the destroyer, in Revelation 9:11.
roots_lines: Hebrew mashchith (H4889) — a destroyer, that which ruins; the destroyer of Exodus 12:23.
Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to corrupt, to spoil, to destroy; the root behind mashchith.
Greek olothreutes (G3644) — the destroyer; used only at 1 Corinthians 10:10.
Greek Apolluon (G623) — Apollyon, the destroyer; the Greek name of the angel of the bottomless pit, called Abaddon in Hebrew (Revelation 9:11).
Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to murmur, to mutter; the sin to which the destroyer was attached.
usage: Will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses (Exodus 12:23) — an agent permitted or forbidden at God’s word.
Were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10) — and the sin named is murmuring.
The same is the companion of a destroyer (Proverbs 28:24) — company a man keeps without choosing it.

etymology: From Old French revenger, from Latin re and vindicare, to claim, to avenge. Webster 1828 distinguishes it sharply from vengeance: revenge is the private return of injury for injury, malicious and forbidden; vengeance is the just infliction of punishment by lawful authority.
biblical_def: Revenge in the Authorized Version follows a distinction the modern ear has lost. Where the word describes what God does, it is righteous: God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies (Nahum 1:2). The triple repetition is not excess but emphasis, opening a book about the destruction of Nineveh. Where the word describes a believer’s zeal against sin discovered in himself, it is commended: Paul lists the fruits of the Corinthians’ godly sorrow and ends with it — what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! (2 Corinthians 7:11). The revenge is against their own former negligence, not against a person. A prophet may ask God to take up his cause: remember me, and visit me, and revenge me of my persecutors (Jeremiah 15:15). But private retaliation between men is flatly forbidden: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD (Leviticus 19:18).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines REVENGE as the return of an injury for an injury, with malice or resentment — a private act, and always criminal in the individual; distinguished from vengeance, the just infliction of punishment by lawful authority or by God.
webster_full: REVENGE, n. — The return of an injury for an injury, in resentment; the deliberate infliction of pain or evil in retaliation.
REVENGE, v.t. — To inflict pain or injury in return for an injury received; to vindicate by punishment.
In the individual, revenge is always criminal, being the effect of malice; God has reserved vengeance to Himself and to the magistrate.
To revenge a cause, in Scripture, is to take up and vindicate the cause of another, as when God avenges His people.
From Latin re and vindico, to claim, to avenge — the root also of vengeance, avenge, and vindicate.
scriptures: Nahum 1:2
God is jealous, and the LORD revengeth; the LORD revengeth, and is furious; the LORD will take vengeance on his adversaries, and he reserveth wrath for his enemies.
2 Corinthians 7:11

For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter.
Leviticus 19:18
Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD.
Romans 12:19
Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.
corruption_summary: Romans 12:19 forbids private revenge on the ground that God will certainly repay, so that the modern reading of forgiveness as the release of the offender from all reckoning removes the very reason the command gives.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s logic is exact and it is often reversed. Avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. The reason the Christian may lay down retaliation is that the debt will be collected by a better Creditor. The modern account of forgiveness usually says the opposite — that letting go means deciding the wrong no longer counts, or that it was smaller than it felt, or that the offender was doing his best. Scripture never asks a wronged person to revise the size of the wrong. It asks him to hand the case to a court that will not fail, which is possible precisely because judgment is real. Hebrews 10:30 repeats the quotation, and Revelation 6:10 has the martyrs asking how long without rebuke.

2 Corinthians 7:11 shows the one direction in which the church may safely turn this energy: against its own sin. The Corinthians had tolerated a scandal; when Paul’s letter produced godly sorrow, it produced indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, and revenge — a settled hostility toward what they had permitted. That is what repentance looks like in a congregation, and it is unmistakably fiercer than the modern process of acknowledging that mistakes were made. Nahum 1:2 supplies the ground beneath both: God is jealous and He repays. A God who did not would leave the wronged with nothing but their own hands.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqam (H5358), to avenge; neqamah (H5360), vengeance; Greek ekdikesis (G1557), vindication, vengeance; ekdikeo (G1556), to vindicate; orge (G3709), wrath.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; the LORD revengeth (Nahum 1:2).
Hebrew neqamah (H5360) — vengeance; To me belongeth vengeance (Deuteronomy 32:35), the verse Paul quotes.
Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — the carrying out of justice; Vengeance is mine; I will repay (Romans 12:19).
Greek ekdikesis in 2 Corinthians 7:11 — rendered revenge, of the church’s zeal against its own tolerated sin.
Greek orge (G3709) — settled wrath; the wrath to which Paul says the believer is to give place.
usage: The LORD revengeth, and is furious (Nahum 1:2) — the just repayment that belongs to God alone.
What zeal, yea, what revenge! (2 Corinthians 7:11) — a church turning this energy against its own tolerated sin.
Avenge not yourselves… Vengeance is mine (Romans 12:19) — retaliation laid down because the debt will be collected.

etymology: From presume, Latin praesumere, to take beforehand, from prae (before) and sumere (to take). Webster 1828: with rash confidence; with arrogance; boldly, without warrant. In the Mosaic law it names the aggravating circumstance that turns an offence into a capital one.
biblical_def: Presumptuously is a legal term in the Mosaic code, marking the difference between sin done in ignorance or weakness and sin done with a high hand. The manslayer who kills unawares may flee to a city of refuge; the man who plans it may not: But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die (Exodus 21:14) — and the altar itself, the last sanctuary, gives him no protection. The same word governs prophecy: if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him (Deuteronomy 18:22). The test is public and the consequence, stated a verse earlier, is death. Israel’s own history furnishes the pattern: refused entry for unbelief, they then attempted the invasion anyway, and Moses records it as the same sin in a new direction — ye would not hear, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD, and went presumptuously up into the hill (Deuteronomy 1:43). Presumption and unbelief are not opposites; they are the same disobedience running the other way.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PRESUMPTUOUSLY as with rash confidence; with arrogant self-reliance; boldly and without authority or warrant; irreverently, in respect to God.
webster_full: PRESUMPTUOUSLY, adv. — With rash confidence; with a bold and arrogant reliance on one’s own judgment or ability.
Without warrant or authority; as, to speak presumptuously in the name of another.
Irreverently, with respect to sacred things; with contempt of divine command.
In the law of Moses, wilfully and with a high hand, as distinguished from sins of ignorance or inadvertence.
From Latin prae, before, and sumo, to take — the root also of presume, presumption, and assume.
scriptures: Exodus 21:14
But if a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour, to slay him with guile; thou shalt take him from mine altar, that he may die.
Deuteronomy 18:22

When a prophet speaketh in the name of the LORD, if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken, but the prophet hath spoken it presumptuously: thou shalt not be afraid of him.
Deuteronomy 1:43
So I spake unto you; and ye would not hear, but rebelled against the commandment of the LORD, and went presumptuously up into the hill.
Deuteronomy 18:20
But the prophet, which shall presume to speak a word in my name, which I have not commanded him to speak, or that shall speak in the name of other gods, even that prophet shall die.
corruption_summary: Deuteronomy 18:20-22 attaches the death penalty to prophecy that fails, and the modern practice of publishing predictions in God’s name and quietly revising them when they do not occur is the exact offence the passage defines.
corruption_paragraphs: The two verses form one law with a test and a penalty. The test is falsifiable: if the thing follow not, nor come to pass, that is the thing which the LORD hath not spoken. The penalty is capital. Israel was not to weigh a prophet’s sincerity, his following, or the general helpfulness of his ministry; one failed word settled it. The modern prophetic movement operates on the reverse principle, treating failed words as the ordinary cost of a gift still being developed, distinguishing prophecy from Scripture in authority so that error is expected, and revising or spiritualising predictions after the fact. Whatever else may be said about the cessation of the sign gifts, this much is plain from the text: God attached lethal seriousness to speaking in His name without warrant, and the church that shrugs at it is not being gracious but disobedient.

Deuteronomy 1:43 identifies the presumption that lives inside religious enthusiasm. Israel had refused to go up when God commanded, and were sentenced to the wilderness; they then went up when God forbade it, and were beaten. The same self-will produced both. Presumption is not the opposite of unbelief but its second act — the will asserting itself against the word of God, first by refusing what is commanded and then by attempting what is not. Exodus 21:14 shows how seriously the law took premeditation: the altar, which sheltered the man who killed unawares, is explicitly stripped from the man who planned it. Deliberateness aggravates, and the sanctuary is no refuge for it.
roots_summary: Hebrew zud (H2102), to act proudly, to boil up, to presume; zadon (H2087), presumptuousness, pride; beyad ramah, with a high hand; Greek tolmetes (G5113), a daring one, presumptuous.
roots_lines: Hebrew zud (H2102) — to seethe, to boil up, and so to act insolently; the man that will do presumptuously (Deuteronomy 17:12).
Hebrew zadon (H2087) — presumption, insolence; the noun of the same root, the pride of thine heart hath deceived thee (Obadiah 1:3).
Hebrew yad ramah — a high hand; the idiom for sin committed openly and in defiance, as against sin of ignorance.
Greek tolmetes (G5113) — a daring, presumptuous man; Presumptuous are they, selfwilled (2 Peter 2:10).
Greek authades (G829) — self-pleasing, arrogant; disqualifying in an elder (Titus 1:7).
usage: If a man come presumptuously upon his neighbour (Exodus 21:14) — premeditation stripping a man of sanctuary.
The prophet hath spoken it presumptuously (Deuteronomy 18:22) — a public, falsifiable test with a capital penalty.
Went presumptuously up into the hill (Deuteronomy 1:43) — the same self-will that had just refused to go.

etymology: From perverse, Latin perversus, turned the wrong way, from per (thoroughly) and vertere (to turn). Webster 1828: disposition to cross or vex; untowardness; crookedness of temper. The root image is a thing turned from its proper direction.
biblical_def: Perverseness names a crookedness of will — not ignorance of the right way but a turning from it — and Scripture locates it in the tongue, in the transgressor’s course, and once, astonishingly, denies it of Israel. Proverbs traces its power to ruin: The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them (Proverbs 11:3). Integrity guides; perverseness destroys; and the two are set as the alternative principles by which a man is carried through life. Proverbs also puts it in speech, with a striking image: A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit (Proverbs 15:4). A crooked word does not merely offend; it breaks something in the hearer. Isaiah lists it among the sins of a nation whose prayers God will not hear: your lips have spoken lies, your tongue hath muttered perverseness (Isaiah 59:3). And then Balaam, hired to curse and unable to, says the thing he did not intend: He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel: the LORD his God is with him, and the shout of a king is among them (Numbers 23:21). Israel was full of perverseness; God, looking at His covenant people, did not see it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PERVERSENESS as disposition to cross or vex; untowardness; crossness; peevishness; petulance; and, more strongly, perversion or crookedness of temper and conduct, a turning from what is right.
webster_full: PERVERSENESS, n. — Disposition to cross or vex; untowardness; crossness of temper.
A disposition that thwarts or opposes what is reasonable or required; obstinacy in the wrong.
Perversion; a turning aside from the right course; crookedness of conduct or of speech.
In Scripture, applied especially to the tongue, as speech that is twisted from truth.
From Latin per, thoroughly, and verto, to turn — the root also of pervert, convert, and subvert.
scriptures: Proverbs 11:3
The integrity of the upright shall guide them: but the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them.
Proverbs 15:4
A wholesome tongue is a tree of life: but perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit.
Isaiah 59:3
For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, your tongue hath muttered perverseness.
Numbers 23:21
He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel: the LORD his God is with him, and the shout of a king is among them.
corruption_summary: Numbers 23:21 says God did not behold iniquity in Jacob at a moment when Jacob was full of it, and the verse is either a sentimental absurdity or the Old Testament’s clearest statement of imputed righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: Balaam speaks these words while Israel is camped in the plains of Moab, weeks from the disaster at Baal-peor that Balaam himself would engineer (Numbers 31:16). The nation is not innocent; the generation that came out of Egypt has already been sentenced to die in the wilderness for unbelief. So the verse cannot mean that God observed no sin. It means that God, regarding His covenant people as covered, did not behold iniquity when He looked at them — which is imputation, seen from the Godward side, long before Romans stated it. Read any other way the verse flatters, and Scripture does not flatter. Read this way it is the ground on which Romans 8:33 stands: Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth.

Proverbs 15:4 addresses a corruption nearer to hand, and it does so with an anatomical bluntness the modern habit of treating speech as harmless cannot match. Perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit — a twisted tongue fractures something in the person it is aimed at. James spends a chapter on the same point, calling the tongue a fire, a world of iniquity, set on fire of hell. Neither writer treats words as a lesser class of action. The dictionary notes the practical consequence for an age of frictionless publication: a crooked sentence now reaches thousands in an hour, and Isaiah 59:3 lists muttered perverseness alongside hands defiled with blood, in one indictment, without apology for the comparison.
roots_summary: Hebrew selaph (H5558), crookedness, perverseness of speech; avon (H5771), iniquity, a twisting; amal (H5999), trouble, mischief; Greek diastrepho (G1294), to twist thoroughly, to pervert.
roots_lines: Hebrew selaph (H5558) — crookedness, distortion; the perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them (Proverbs 11:3).
Hebrew amal (H5999) — toil, mischief, trouble; the word behind perverseness in Numbers 23:21.
Hebrew avon (H5771) — iniquity, from a root meaning to bend or twist; the companion term in the same verse.
Greek diastrepho (G1294) — to distort, to turn aside; O faithless and perverse generation (Matthew 17:17).
Greek skolios (G4646) — crooked, bent; a crooked and perverse nation (Philippians 2:15), and the root of scoliosis.
usage: The perverseness of transgressors shall destroy them (Proverbs 11:3) — the alternative principle to integrity.
Perverseness therein is a breach in the spirit (Proverbs 15:4) — a crooked word fractures something in the hearer.
Neither hath he seen perverseness in Israel (Numbers 23:21) — imputation seen from the Godward side.

etymology: From Old French desfier, to renounce faith or allegiance, from Latin dis and fidus, faithful. Webster 1828: challenged to combat; dared; braved. The word originally meant to renounce one’s pledged faith, and so to declare oneself an enemy.
biblical_def: Defied in Scripture belongs above all to the valley of Elah, where a giant challenged an army and a shepherd understood who had really been challenged. David’s statement is the theological centre of the whole account: Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:36). Saul and the army heard a defiance of Israel; David heard a defiance of the God whose armies these were, and that single reframing is why he alone was not afraid. The Chronicler records the same word of a later giant: But when he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea David’s brother slew him (1 Chronicles 20:7) — the pattern continued into the next generation, and so did the answer. Balaam supplies the other and decisive use, when Balak has hired him to curse and he finds he cannot: How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied? (Numbers 23:8). A hired prophet discovers that defiance of a covenant people is impossible unless God defies them first, which is the same doctrine David preached with a sling.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DEFIED as challenged to combat; dared; braved; set at nought or treated with contempt, as an authority or a threatened evil.
webster_full: DEFIED, pp. — Challenged to combat; dared to an encounter.
Braved; set at defiance; treated with contempt or bold opposition.
Provoked to action by a challenge, especially a public one.
In its oldest sense, having renounced faith or allegiance to; hence, having declared oneself an enemy.
From Old French desfier, from Latin dis and fides, faith — the root also of defiance, fidelity, and infidel.
scriptures: 1 Samuel 17:36
Thy servant slew both the lion and the bear: and this uncircumcised Philistine shall be as one of them, seeing he hath defied the armies of the living God.
1 Chronicles 20:7
But when he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea David's brother slew him.
Numbers 23:8
How shall I curse, whom God hath not cursed? or how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied?
1 Samuel 17:28

And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle.
corruption_summary: David and Goliath is preached almost universally as a lesson in courage against personal obstacles, which turns the one man in the story who was not the hero’s equal into a metaphor and quietly removes the covenant argument David actually made.
corruption_paragraphs: The moralised reading is so common it needs stating plainly: the giants in your life are not Goliath, and you are not David. David is the anointed of the LORD, standing as the champion of a people who could not fight for themselves, defeating an enemy in single combat so that the victory is reckoned to the whole nation — which is a picture of Christ, not a template for self-confidence. David’s own reasoning in 1 Samuel 17:36 is covenantal, not motivational: the Philistine is uncircumcised, he has defied the armies of the living God, and therefore he will fall as the lion and the bear fell. Remove the covenant and the sentence loses its logic; what remains is a story about believing in yourself, which is the opposite of what David said.

Numbers 23:8 states the underlying principle and states it from the mouth of a man who wanted it to be otherwise. Balaam had been paid to curse Israel and discovered that he could not defy whom the LORD had not defied. The security of God’s people rests on God’s own disposition toward them, not on their merit — Israel was in no better spiritual condition that day than on any other — and no hostile power, hired or volunteer, can alter it. Paul turns exactly this into the great question of Romans 8: If God be for us, who can be against us? The Old Testament had already answered it in the mouth of a false prophet who tried and failed.
roots_summary: Hebrew charaph (H2778), to reproach, to defy, to taunt; cherpah (H2781), reproach; zaam (H2194), to be indignant, to defy; Greek oneidizo (G3679), to reproach, to revile.
roots_lines: Hebrew charaph (H2778) — to reproach, to taunt, to defy; he hath defied the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:36).
Hebrew cherpah (H2781) — reproach, shame; take away the reproach from Israel (1 Samuel 17:26).
Hebrew zaam (H2194) — to be indignant, to denounce; how shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied? (Numbers 23:8).
Greek oneidizo (G3679) — to reproach, to revile; used of the reproaches that fell on Christ (Romans 15:3).
Hebrew arel (H6189) — uncircumcised; David’s decisive description of Goliath, a covenant category rather than an insult.
usage: He hath defied the armies of the living God (1 Samuel 17:36) — the reframing that made David unafraid.
When he defied Israel… Jonathan the son of Shimea… slew him (1 Chronicles 20:7) — the pattern repeating in the next generation.
How shall I defy, whom the LORD hath not defied? (Numbers 23:8) — a hired prophet discovering he could not.

etymology: From rob, Old French rober, to plunder, of Germanic origin. Webster 1828: the forcible or felonious taking of goods from the person of another. Philippians 2:6 uses the Greek harpagmos, a thing seized or grasped at, in a construction that has been fought over since the fourth century.
biblical_def: Robbery appears in Scripture in three settings, and the third is one of the great Christological texts. In the psalm it is a warning against a whole way of getting: Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them (Psalm 62:10). Not merely do not rob — do not become vain in it, since the man who lives by taking begins to think of himself as clever rather than as a thief. In Isaiah it is worship built on plunder, which God says He hates: For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them (Isaiah 61:8). An offering funded by theft insults the God it is meant to honour. And in Philippians the word describes what Christ did not do: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God (Philippians 2:6). Being in the form of God, equality with God was not a thing He had to seize, because it was already His — and the verses that follow describe Him laying aside not His deity but its manifest privileges, taking the form of a servant, and becoming obedient unto death.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ROBBERY as the forcible or felonious taking of anything from the person of another, or in his presence, against his will, by violence or by putting him in fear; and, more generally, the taking away by unlawful means what belongs to another.
webster_full: ROBBERY, n. — The forcible or felonious taking of goods from the person of another, or in his presence, against his will, by violence or by putting him in fear.
In a general sense, the taking away by unlawful force or artifice what rightfully belongs to another.
Plunder; spoil; the thing taken by violence.
Figuratively, a seizing or grasping at what one has no right to hold.
From Old French rober, to plunder — the root also of rob, robber, and, through the sense of stripping, of robe.
scriptures: Psalm 62:10
Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them.
Isaiah 61:8
For I the LORD love judgment, I hate robbery for burnt offering; and I will direct their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them.
Philippians 2:6
Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God:
Proverbs 28:24
Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer.
corruption_summary: Philippians 2:6 has been made to carry a kenotic Christology in which the Son emptied Himself of divine attributes at the incarnation, and the Watchtower reads the same verse as proof that He never possessed equality with God at all.
corruption_paragraphs: The kenotic theories of the nineteenth century — Thomasius, Gess, and their English followers — took made himself of no reputation (literally, emptied Himself) in verse 7 to mean that the Son surrendered omniscience, omnipotence, or omnipresence in becoming man. This cannot stand with Chalcedon or with the text. Verse 6 says He was in the form of God and did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped at; verse 7 says He emptied Himself by taking the form of a servant. The emptying is an addition, not a subtraction: He took manhood, He did not lay down Godhead. A deity that can be set aside is not deity, and Colossians 2:9 says that in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily — present tense, of the incarnate Christ.

The Watchtower and other Arian readings run the other way, taking thought it not robbery to mean that Christ did not presume to grasp at an equality that was never His. But the clause is governed by being in the form of God, and the whole passage argues from what He was to what He was willing to become; there is no argument at all if He was a creature declining to overreach. Paul’s pastoral point in Philippians 2 depends on the height of the descent: the Corinthians are told to have this mind because the One who was equal with God took a servant’s form and a criminal’s death. Isaiah 61:8 supplies the practical corollary for the church — God hates worship funded by what was taken from someone.
roots_summary: Greek harpagmos (G725), a thing seized or to be grasped at; harpazo (G726), to seize by force; Hebrew gazel (H1498), robbery, that which is taken by violence; gazal (H1497), to tear away, to plunder.
roots_lines: Greek harpagmos (G725) — a thing snatched, or the act of snatching; the disputed word of Philippians 2:6.
Greek harpazo (G726) — to seize, to carry off by force; used of the catching up of the saints (1 Thessalonians 4:17).
Hebrew gazel (H1498) — robbery, plunder; I hate robbery for burnt offering (Isaiah 61:8).
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to seize violently; the root of gazel.
Greek kenoo (G2758) — to empty; made himself of no reputation (Philippians 2:7), the verb behind the kenotic controversy.
usage: Become not vain in robbery (Psalm 62:10) — the danger is not only the theft but the self-regard it breeds.
I hate robbery for burnt offering (Isaiah 61:8) — worship funded by plunder insults the God it honours.
Thought it not robbery to be equal with God (Philippians 2:6) — not a thing to be seized, because already His.

etymology: From dark, Saxon deorc. Webster 1828: made dark; deprived of light; obscured; rendered dim or gloomy. Scripture uses it of the sun at judgment, of the failing eye in old age, and above all of the understanding of men who suppressed what they knew of God.
biblical_def: Darkened in the New Testament is chiefly a description of the fallen mind, and Paul uses it twice with clinical precision. Romans traces the sequence: Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened (Romans 1:21). The order is critical. The darkening is not the starting point but the result — they knew, they refused to glorify, they refused thanks, and then the heart was darkened. Suppression of known truth issues in incapacity to see it. Ephesians states the same condition as the settled state of the unregenerate: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart (Ephesians 4:18), and again the ignorance is traced back to a blindness of heart rather than a want of evidence. The word also belongs to the last day, when the created lights fail at the coming of the Son of man: Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven (Matthew 24:29).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DARKENED as made dark; deprived of light; obscured; rendered dim, gloomy, or less clear; and figuratively, rendered ignorant, blind, or unintelligible.
webster_full: DARKENED, pp. — Made dark; deprived of light; obscured; made dim or gloomy.
Rendered less clear or intelligible; obscured in meaning; as, counsel darkened by words without knowledge.
Rendered blind or ignorant; deprived of spiritual or intellectual light.
Sullied; made less white or bright; clouded, as a countenance or a reputation.
From Saxon deorc, dark — the root also of darkness, darkling, and darksome.
scriptures: Romans 1:21
Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened.
Ephesians 4:18
Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:
Matthew 24:29
Immediately after the tribulation of those days shall the sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light, and the stars shall fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens shall be shaken:
Isaiah 59:3
For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, your tongue hath muttered perverseness.
corruption_summary: Romans 1:21 says the darkening of the mind followed the refusal to glorify and give thanks, which contradicts the standing assumption that unbelief is fundamentally an intellectual problem awaiting better arguments.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul’s account is moral before it is intellectual, and the sequence cannot be rearranged. Men knew God; they did not glorify Him as God; they were not thankful; their reasonings became vain; the heart was darkened; professing themselves wise they became fools. Ingratitude appears in the chain before idolatry, which is worth sitting with. This is the ground of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity as it touches the mind: the noetic effects of sin mean that the unbeliever is not a neutral inquirer weighing evidence but a man suppressing what he already has. It also tells the church what apologetics can and cannot do. Arguments are worth making and Paul made them at Athens, but no argument regenerates; God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Ephesians 4:18 forecloses the other common view, that people are lost merely for want of information. Paul says the ignorance is in them and that it proceeds from the blindness of their heart — the organ named is not the intellect but the affections and the will. This does not make evangelism pointless; it makes it dependent. The same apostle who wrote these verses spent his life preaching, because faith comes by hearing and God is pleased to give sight through the foolishness of preaching. Matthew 24:29 sets the whole matter against its final horizon: the day comes when the created lights are darkened and no argument is needed, because the Son of man will be seen.
roots_summary: Greek skotizo (G4654), to darken, to obscure; skotos (G4655), darkness; skotoo (G4656), to be darkened; Hebrew chashak (H2821), to be dark, to grow dim.
roots_lines: Greek skotizo (G4654) — to darken; their foolish heart was darkened (Romans 1:21) and the sun be darkened (Matthew 24:29).
Greek skotoo (G4656) — to be darkened, to be blinded; having the understanding darkened (Ephesians 4:18).
Greek skotos (G4655) — darkness; the realm from which the saints are called into marvellous light (1 Peter 2:9).
Hebrew chashak (H2821) — to be or grow dark; those that look out of the windows be darkened (Ecclesiastes 12:3).
Greek porosis (G4457) — hardness, callousness; the blindness of their heart in Ephesians 4:18 is literally a callus.
usage: Their foolish heart was darkened (Romans 1:21) — the darkening follows the refusal to glorify and give thanks.
Having the understanding darkened… because of the blindness of their heart (Ephesians 4:18) — the organ named is the heart.
The sun be darkened, and the moon shall not give her light (Matthew 24:29) — the created lights failing at His coming.
